title: The Fifty Nairobi Women Who Would Not Let Ingrid Munro Retire
dek: In 1999 a retiring Swedish architect in Nairobi agreed to keep working with fifty women who begged, on condition that they saved first; it was the start of Jamii Bora.

story.event: Starting a savings and loan scheme with fifty women who begged on Nairobi's streets
story.summary: In 1999, as Swedish architect Ingrid Munro prepared to retire from heading the African Housing Fund in Nairobi, fifty women who begged on the streets and had worked with her asked her not to leave. She agreed on condition that they saved, promising they could borrow two shillings for every shilling saved; the women named the group Jamii Bora, 'good families'. By 2007 it had about 170,000 members and was Kenya's largest microfinance organisation.
paragraphs: In 1999 Ingrid Munro, a Swedish architect who headed the African Housing Fund in Nairobi, was due to retire. She and her Canadian husband, Bob, had adopted a boy who had lived on the streets, and later his two brothers, and through them she had come to know many of the city's poorest families. Fifty women who begged on the streets, many of them mothers, had worked with her on a housing project in the slums. When they heard she was leaving, they followed her and told her, as she later recounted to Svenska Dagbladet, that a mother cannot retire.

She stayed, but not on their terms. After fourteen years in Africa, she said, she had learned that charity does not lift people out of poverty. So she set a condition: if they wanted her to do something for them, they would have to do something for themselves. A good mother, she told them, also wants her children to stand on their own. Her offer: save what you can, even as beggars, and you will be able to borrow two shillings for every shilling you put aside.

Two months later the group came back with 8,000 shillings and received 16,000 in loans. The money went into small trades: vegetable stalls, selling charcoal, collecting paper for recycling. Among the fifty was Janet Bett, a trained teacher who had spent three years homeless with her six children; because she could read and spoke English and Swahili, she translated and helped run the group's affairs. The name came from the women. One day, Munro said, they told her she was the only one who understood that they too were good mothers. They called themselves Jamii Bora, Swahili for good families, and the trust was founded on 22 November 1999.

The first fifty became its first social workers, going back to the streets to find others who wanted to follow them. When members kept falling behind on loans because someone at home was ill, the trust added health insurance. By 2007 it had about 170,000 members, the largest microfinance organisation in Kenya. Munro kept long days, leaving for work at half past six, but she told the same newspaper in 2009 that Sundays belonged to her grandchildren.

quote.text: We were warned against indulging in indiscriminate charity, without seasoning it with justice and rectitude. Masamuné expressed it well in his oft-quoted aphorism—“Rectitude carried to excess hardens into stiffness; Benevolence indulged beyond measure sinks into weakness.”
quote.locator: Chapter V, "Benevolence, the Feeling of Distress"
quote.source_title: Bushido, the Soul of Japan, Project Gutenberg eBook #12096
quote.connection: Nitobe calls benevolence mother-like, then warns that it weakens without justice to season it. Munro's two shillings for every one saved was that balance in practice: help that was real and generous, and that still asked the women to carry their own share.

reflection: Munro's condition was not a test of whether the women deserved help. She had already decided they did. It was a way of making the help last: money they had saved themselves, then doubled, belonged to them in a way a gift would not.

You are probably asked for help often, by colleagues, by family, by people who know you are capable. Yes is easy to say and no is hard. There is a third answer, quieter than both: a yes that leaves a part for the other person to carry. It treats them as able, and it spares you from carrying everything alone.
invitation: Think of one request for help that is waiting on you. Before you take it on, decide the one first step the other person could take themselves, and ask them for it kindly.

cross_checks.claim: In 1999, as she retired from the African housing body, Munro began working with fifty women who had begged on the streets.
The rule was to save first and borrow twice what was saved (two shillings per shilling).
Munro made her help conditional on the women doing something for themselves: she would provide a ladder, but they had to climb it.
Janet Bett was one of the first fifty and helped run the group.
By 2007 Jamii Bora had about 170,000 members.
Health insurance was added because illness in members' families was behind missed repayments.

research_notes: The founding episode rests mainly on two Svenska Dagbladet interviews with Munro (2007 and 2009, in Swedish); her words and the women's are given in reported speech, translated, rather than in quotation marks. Organisation name: SvD 2007, The Standard and others call her employer the African Housing Fund; SvD 2009 and Wikipedia call it the African Housing Foundation; the story uses 'Fund'. Her time in Africa: SvD 2007 quotes her as saying she had been fourteen years in Africa by then; the story gives that figure as hers and does not state how long she held the housing post. How she met the women: SvD 2009 says they had worked with her on a slum housing project; IMD says the mothers of her adopted sons' friends sought her out; the story gives both as complementary. Membership: SvD 2007 and IMD give about 170,000 in 2007; Dagen and SvD 2009 give about or more than 200,000 by 2009; oikos says nearly 200,000; a Grameen America blog claims 250,000; IMD says it peaked above 300,000. The story uses the 2007 figure, which two sources agree on. Founding date: The Standard (2017) gives 22 November 1999; oikos says late 1999. The IMD feature wrongly says the trust was founded in 2010; it is cited only for Janet Bett's story, the savings rule and the 2007 membership figure. The amount of the first loans (8,000 shillings saved, 16,000 received after two months) appears only in SvD 2007, from Munro's account to that paper; no other source gives a different figure. Later history: Jamii Bora's lending moved into a commercial bank in 2010, whose later difficulties are reported but not well documented in loadable sources; the story deliberately stops at the trust's first years. Quote: Nitobe wrote in English, so no translator is given; the aphorism inside it is attributed by Nitobe to Masamuné (Date Masamune).
